experiment.title: Does routing by our own rulebook beat one fixed model on real tasks?
experiment.summary: Odin's routing rulebook (rule 27) says which model tier a task deserves. We turn the rulebook, as it is now written, into a frozen table that picks one model per task, and compare it with two fixed choices on the same eight real coding tasks from our own repository: always our strongest-value model (Claude Opus 5.5) and always our cheapest proven one (GPT-6 Luna). Each arm does every task three times in a sealed sandbox. The headline is what each arm pays per hidden test case it makes pass.
experiment.note: Written, hashed and merged to main before any counted cell. Nothing in this record may change afterwards; a later change is a new, dated amendment, published first.

question: Is a cell routed by the rulebook's frozen table cheaper per case fixed than always using one fixed model, without fixing a smaller share of the cases? Asked twice: against fixed Opus 5.5 and against fixed GPT-6 Luna. The claim under test is narrow: 'routing as now specified' — a table copied from our written rule, not a learned or per-request router.

arms.plan: the table's classifier reads each task's declared source files: one file -> openai/gpt-6-luna (3 tasks); two or more -> openai/gpt-6-sol (4 tasks); a file path naming authentication or credential handling -> anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 (1 task). The plan is fixed before the run and asserted by a test in the engineering repository.

corpus.name: odin-replay-v1
corpus.boundary: Eight real merged changes from our private engineering repository (2026-09-08..09-23), each replayed from its parent commit. The model gets the change's work order; the change's own hidden tests then run against what it wrote. Only counts are published: no task names, numbers, titles, paths or contents. A cell's score is the share of the target cases (hidden test cases that failed before the original change and passed after it) that the model's change makes pass.
corpus.selection: All 8 tasks of the corpus, including the 2 that the 2026-09-24 run did not measure. The corpus selection gate (each task's hidden tests fail on the parent and pass on the merge, under the grading sandbox) predates this experiment.

design.cells: 3 arms x 8 tasks x 3 replicates = 72 cells.
design.lanes: 9 lanes, one per arm x replicate, each on its own dedicated OpenRouter key used for nothing else. Within a lane the 8 tasks run one at a time in corpus order; lanes run in parallel.
design.cell: A fresh history-free clone at the task's parent commit (the original change is not reachable), the agent odin-agent 6.88.22 run headless with a 25-minute limit inside an OS sandbox whose only network is openrouter.ai, then grading of the hidden tests inside the sandbox with no network. One attempt per cell; no re-runs.
design.agentPin: odin-agent 6.88.22, copied to a frozen directory before the run; the driver refuses any other version. The 2026-09-24 run used 6.88.2; the registry's newest is 6.89.2. Not the same agent as that run.

harness.privateCode: The cells are driven by the private replay bench of Odin's engineering repository, at the commit named below on its main branch (odin-labs-ai/odin-labs #8458, merged 2026-10-23), in a detached checkout not edited during the run. Published here as hashes.

metric.perReplicate: For one arm x replicate: cases fixed = the sum of target cases fixed over its graded cells; share = cases fixed / target cases of its graded cells; billed = the arm x replicate key's usage after minus before (OpenRouter's own counter, read once before the first cell and again at least 90 s after the last); $ per case fixed = billed / cases fixed.
metric.perArm: The mean over complete replicates of $ per case fixed with its 95% Student-t interval (df = 2 for three replicates, t = 4.303, so the interval will be wide); the mean share with its interval; the share range (largest minus smallest replicate share); the pooled $ per case fixed (all billed / all cases fixed); total billed.
metric.graded: A cell is graded unless it is recorded as error: cut by a spend cap, no model response, or a sandbox escape. Error cells are reported in a shortfall count, never imputed. A replicate is complete when all 8 of its cells are graded.
metric.outOfSample: Reported separately per arm: the share of target cases fixed on the 2 tasks the 2026-09-24 run did not measure, pooled over replicates. No $ for this row: one replicate's bill cannot be split by task.

decision.rule: Routing beats fixed X if its mean $ per case fixed is lower AND its mean share is not lower than X's by more than the replicate spread. The replicate spread is the larger of the two arms' share ranges. Evaluated separately for X = Opus and X = Luna.
decision.incomplete: If either arm of a comparison has fewer than 3 complete replicates, that comparison is 'incomplete' and reported with its finished counts. Nothing is extrapolated.
decision.consistency: On the one task the table routes to Opus 5.5, the router and the fixed-Opus arms run the same model on the same task; their cells there are a built-in check of run-to-run noise and are reported, not judged.

calibration.disclosed: The 2026-09-24 clean run (odin-agent 6.88.2, one run per task, 6 of these 8 tasks) measured, among others: Opus 5.5 140/200 target cases (70.0%) at $4.30 per task; GPT-6 Sol 135/200 (67.5%) at $2.99; GPT-6 Luna 118/200 (59.0%) at $0.89. The table's picks are taken from that run, so on those 6 tasks the router arm is in-sample: its models were chosen on the tasks they are scored on. Only 2 tasks are out-of-sample. A spike on 2026-10-23 ran one cell of the earlier table (v1, title keywords) in the sandbox: 2 of 5 target cases, $0.24 billed. The v1 table sent 4 of 8 tasks to a premium model; v2 sends 1.
calibration.prediction: From the 2026-09-24 figures: router about $21 per replicate, Opus about $34, Luna about $6. Router beats fixed Opus (cheaper at a similar share); router does not beat fixed Luna (Luna is cheaper per case fixed). Written down so the result can contradict it.

analysis.inputs: data/cells.json and data/billing.json, written by the private export script (hash above) from the run's evidence: per cell its arm, replicate, an opaque task index (t1..t8), whether it is out-of-sample, the model, verdict and target cases fixed / total; per lane its key's usage before and after.
analysis.check: node experiments/router-arm/analyse.mjs --check exits 0 only if results.json is exactly what the frozen script computes from the committed inputs.

spend.keys: Nine dedicated OpenRouter keys with lifetime limits: Opus lanes $50 each, router lanes $30 each, Luna lanes $11 each, $273 in total. Each key's limit is the hard ceiling of its lane: OpenRouter refuses calls past it. The per-key limits exceed the minting policy's usual $30 per key per day; the authority is the founder's decision of 2026-10-23 approving this replay with a hard $275 cap.
spend.runnerStop: Each lane's driver also stops before a cell once its own spend reading reaches the lane cap less $1 (REPLAY_MAX_USD). That reading under-counts until OpenRouter settles, which is why the key limit, not the driver, is the ceiling.
spend.accountGuard: A lane stops before a cell when the shared OpenRouter account has less than $100 left, so the run cannot starve the rest of the company's traffic.
spend.expected: About $185 in total, from the 2026-09-24 per-task figures.
spend.stop: A lane that hits its cap, its key limit or the account guard stops; its unfinished cells are reported as missing and the replicate as incomplete. Nothing is re-run past a cap.

notBefore: The first counted cell is started after this record is merged to main of odin-labs-ai/odin-rnd. The merge is the freeze.
limits: Eight tasks from one repository and one work family (shell and Node operations scripts with their own tests). It says nothing about other kinds of work.
The router is in-sample on 6 of 8 tasks: its picks come from a run on those tasks. The out-of-sample row covers 2 tasks only.
Three replicates. Replicates repeat the same tasks, so the intervals describe run-to-run variation, not variation across tasks; with df = 2 they are wide.
One broker (OpenRouter); it chooses the upstream host per request.
The claim is about routing as written today: a frozen copy of our rule, not a learned or per-request router, and not the gateway's automatic ranker, which the sandbox cannot reach.
The corpus is private: readers can check the hashes, method, counts and costs, but cannot rerun the tasks.
